title: England's Toprak wins judo gold with golden score
description: England judoka Acelya Toprak overcomes India's Yamini Mourya in the women's -57kg final to win gold at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
England's Acelya Toprak overcame India's Yamini Mourya in the women's -57kg judo final to win the gold medal at the Commonwealth Games.

In an exhausting bout that went to golden score and lasted almost seven minutes, Toprak eventually forced Mourya into a third shido to claim victory.

The 28-year-old had won silver in 2022 but managed to go one better this time around in Glasgow.

"My last Commonwealth Games went exactly the same way. In the final it was two shidos each, we were into four-and-a-half minutes of extra time and I made that one misstep, over-stretched and got caught," Toprak told BBC Sport.

"So I'm very happy that this time I didn't do that, because that's shattering, that hurts.

"All you're thinking about is get up and go again, get up and go again, and then after I was like 'I like a golden score in the finals, don't I?'

"You're exhausted, someone's trying to throw you on your head for eight minutes and you've just got to get up and go again."

It was an excellent night for England's judo athletes with all five who were in medal contention winning their matches.

Lele Nairne, who was beaten by Toprak in the women's -57kg semi-final, won bronze by ippon with an emphatic throw to the mat to defeat Ghanaian 17-year-old Frema Agyei within just 28 seconds.

"I love throwing people like that," Nairne, 28, said after her victory.

"I love it. It's a bittersweet symphony. Birmingham [2022] was tragic, I lost to a good friend in the bronze medal match, so I wanted to redeem myself.

"I wanted a medal, I wanted a gold, but just to get a medal, I'm absolutely over the moon."

Tatum Keen - Nairne's training partner at Bradley Stoke Judo Club in Bristol - also won bronze in the women's -52kg category.

And in the men's judo, 20-year-old Charlie Ayre and Michael Fryer, 26, claimed bronze in their respective -60kg and -66kg events.

title: Cricket & archery well placed for Commonwealths spot
description: Cricket, archery and shooting are among the sports well placed to regain their spot at the Commonwealth Games in India in 2030.
fullText:
Cricket, archery and shooting are among the sports well placed to regain their spot at the Commonwealth Games in India in 2030.

Only 10 sports were included in the ongoing Glasgow Games because of the rushed build-up after the Australian state of Victoria pulled out as hosts.

Discussions on the sporting programme remain ongoing between Commonwealth Sport, sporting federations and the Indian organising committee for the next Games, which will be held in Ahmedabad, Gujarat.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Commonwealth Sport chief executive Katie Sadlier would not be drawn on the process but India Olympic Association's Raghu Iyer said: "There are many sports who will feel they have missed out.

"There are sports in which India has done very well, shooting, archery and many other sports."

Pushed on whether that puts cricket, which was included for Birmingham 2022 for the first time in 24 years as a women's-only T20 event, archery and shooting at the top of the queue, Iyer added: "While I do not have the mandate to talk about any of these, you have been pretty interesting with the choices you have mentioned…"

"We also want to have sports that India have traditionally done well in," he said.

Boxer Abdul - grandson of dictator - disqualified for headbutt

Cricket's cause is helped by the fact at least two team sports will be added for 2030. Hockey and rugby sevens would be other options.

Badminton, 3x3 basketball and 3x3 wheelchair basketball, beach volleyball, cycling, diving, judo, rhythmic gymnastics, squash, triathlon and para triathlon and wrestling are other sports under consideration.

India can also propose two new sports as host nation and push others that have significance at home. No final decisions have been made.

Ahmedabad will be the Commonwealth's centenary Games and events will held in the 120,000-seater Narendra Modi Stadium, which has hosted two cricket World Cup finals in recent years.

India has also expressed a keen interest in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games, with this potentially a key step in the road.

"Any sporting event will be a step towards that," Iyer said. "We are looking purely at ensuring that these Commonwealth Games are one of the best that have been held."

The reduced programme in Glasgow has helped slash the cost of hosting the Games from around £800m to £160m.

Organisers have been keen to claim this repurposed structure will be cheaper and more appealing for future hosts, but the sporting programme will rise to 17 in Ahmedabad.

"17 is, we think, the right number," Sadlier said.

"The Victoria Games was 26 sports. We recognised we needed to reset and bring the Games into something that was affordable around the Commonwealth.

"What we have done here has been brilliant but we will bring back a few sports. We won't go beyond that number."

Sadlier also rejected concerns around the cut through of the Glasgow Games, given there has been no live television coverage on a major channel in the UK.

"We have got more broadcast deals signed for this Games than we ever have," she said.

"Globally, the reach has been exceptional. On socials we broke the targets from Birmingham last week. It has been an amazingly covered Games."

title: Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah 'spring chicken': Australia legend tells India pacer to increase longevity
description: Aussie legend Glenn McGrath called Jasprit Bumrah a 'spring chicken' and shared key workload advice for the Indian pacer to maximize his career longevity.
fullText:
Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah 'spring chicken': Australia legend tells India pacer to increase longevity originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Glenn McGrath calls Jasprit Bumrah, 32, still young and urges format prioritisation.

Recent injuries hit India's pace unit, including Bumrah and Prince Yadav.

McGrath urges bowlers to build strength, not caution, against breakdowns.

Australian pace legend Glenn McGrath has weighed in on Jasprit Bumrah's ongoing fitness concerns and described the Indian spearhead as a 'spring chicken' who is still relatively young in cricketing terms. However, he suggested that Bumrah might need to figure out a way to stretch his career further, potentially by cutting back his workload in one of the three formats.

Ever since the international calendar resumed following the IPL back in June, India's fast bowling stocks have been repeatedly tested by injuries. Bumrah's own participation in the upcoming Test series against Sri Lanka remains uncertain, while fellow pacer Prince Yadav also picked up an injury during the recent Zimbabwe tour.

Mayank Yadav only recently returned to international duty after being sidelined for two years, and given India's packed year-round schedule, the team management has increasingly leaned on a rotation strategy to manage player workloads.

MORE: Laxman praises Sooryavanshi's maturity after heroics vs Zimbabwe

McGrath, who works with the MRF Pace Foundation, said the decision on how to manage Bumrah's career will ultimately rest with the bowler himself.

“Well again it’s up to him what he wants. How old’s Bumrah now? 31- 32? He’s only a spring chicken. So he’s got to find a way to have a bit of longevity," he said.

According to McGrath, much of the path forward depends on what Bumrah himself wants, whether that means prioritising Test cricket or shifting focus more toward the shorter formats, alongside how his body continues to respond over time.

"He’s had a few injuries unfortunately, but he’s class, a quality bowler. Just see what he wants to do," McGrath said.

"That’s what it comes down to: whether he wants to focus on Test cricket or whether he just wants to play T20. It also depends on his body. And like I said, guys who hyper-extend their arm do place a bit more stress through that joint there. So we’ll see what the future holds."

MORE: 'Abhishek sorted out': Srikkanth believes Samson will return to India T20I side

Beyond Bumrah specifically, McGrath used the opportunity to share broader thoughts on how fast bowlers are managed in the modern game, arguing that players should be conditioned to handle the physical demands of pace bowling rather than being overly shielded from potential breakdowns.

“It’s the nature of the beast being a fast bowler; it’s not a natural action so injuries are part of the game,” McGrath said.

"Where I’m a little disappointed these days, and it’s probably been that way a little bit for a long time, is that they put them (fast bowlers) in cotton wool. We try to nurse them back to full fitness, and we protect them."

MORE: Why is 33-year-old Saransh Jain included in India Test squad for SL tour

In his view, extended rehabilitation stints often do more harm than good, since months spent recovering can leave a player's overall fitness and strength trailing far behind where it needs to be.

"The best way to do it is to get stronger than the stresses of fast bowling. To do a rehab program for months and months puts your fitness and your strength so far behind that you’ve got so far to catch up."

After tearing his side muscle and dropping to just 77 kilograms, McGrath said he realised a change was necessary if he wanted a sustainable career, a turning point that led him to work closely with trainer Kevin Chevell, who helped make him considerably more durable over time.

"Getting physically stronger and fitter doesn’t mean bowling hours in the nets or working on the wrong things in the gym," McGrath opined.

"I got stronger than the stresses of fast bowling and very rarely got injured. So instead of putting him in cotton wool, we should be actually making him unbreakable, getting him working hard.

"When I tore my side muscle, I lost a heap of weight. I weighed 77 kilograms, so I realised if I keep doing what I’m doing, I’m not going to last very long. That’s why I went down the train and Kevin Chevell (training), who’s working here with the boys and he made me unbreakable."

MORE: 'How can I plan?': Samson on his India future at 2028 T20 WC amid Sooryavanshi's rise

McGrath's stance carries weight given his own remarkable longevity, but applying his era's approach directly to today's game overlooks how drastically fast bowlers' schedules have changed.

Modern quicks like Bumrah juggle franchise cricket, bilateral series and global tournaments almost year-round, a workload McGrath never had to manage across three formats simultaneously. Building physical resilience is undeniably important, but so is smart load management in a calendar this congested, something India's rotation policy already attempts to address rather than pure over-caution.

Bumrah's hyper-extension action also isn't comparable to a standard side strain, it's a structural factor that genuinely increases injury risk regardless of conditioning levels. McGrath's broader point about strength training holds value, but reducing Bumrah's fitness challenges purely to a mindset issue risks oversimplifying a much more complex modern problem.

'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
description: The education minister's resignation, a rare setback for the Modi government, brings hope to many young protesters that their voices will be heard.
fullText:
In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct.

So the resignation of education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, on Saturday after more than a week of intense street demonstrations was a defining moment – and one which many young people were quick to celebrate.

In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests".

Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit.

Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years".

On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times.

Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram."

The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.

The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families.

Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk.

Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them.

The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country.

Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed.

Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning".

"For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says.

Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage.

Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded.

"Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says.

Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture.

India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data.

Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs.

The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year.

On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended.

"I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices."

Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over."

A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next".

But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension.

Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees".

But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations.

Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40.

The organisation Human Rights Watch says that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws".

Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual".

At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scripts history, becomes first player to achieve unique T20I feat before turning 16
description: The left-handed opener achieved the feat during the third and final T20I against Zimbabwe in Harare on Sunday, scoring 81 off 48 balls to lead India to 192/5 after they elected to bat first.
fullText:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi continued to rewrite records as the 15-year-old became only the first player in men's international cricket to register multiple scores of 50 or more before turning 16.

The left-handed opener achieved the feat during the third and final T20I against Zimbabwe in Harare on Sunday, scoring 81 off 48 balls to lead India to 192/5 after they elected to bat first.

Only Nepal's Kushal Malla had previously recorded a 50-plus score in men's internationals before turning 16. Sooryavanshi has now gone one better with two such scores to his name.

50-plus scores before turning 16 in Men’s internationals

2 - Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (India)

On a pitch that offered assistance to the bowlers, Sooryavanshi showed a different side to his batting. He began cautiously, scoring 11 runs from his first 10 balls and 26 from his first 20 deliveries before bringing up his second T20I fifty in 31 balls.

His innings still included some of the strokeplay that has become his trademark. He drove Brad Evans straight down the ground for four off a yorker and later launched off-spinner Sikandar Raza for a 102-metre six. He also reverse-swept Wesley Madhevere for a boundary.

While Sooryavanshi settled in, opening partner Abhishek Sharma's lean run continued. Abhishek edged Blessing Muzarabani to wicketkeeper Tadi Marumani for two, extending his sequence of low scores. His last six innings have produced 10, 16, 3, 1, 8 and 2, dating back to the third T20I against England in Nottingham last month.

Sooryavanshi then added 75 runs for the second wicket with Ishan Kishan, who made 29, before sharing a 50-run partnership with captain Shreyas Iyer, who scored 27.

The youngster looked set for a century before Wesley Madhevere dismissed him. Brad Evans completed a catch at long-off to end his innings on 81.

India could not maintain the same scoring rate after the departures of Sooryavanshi and Shreyas. The middle order added only 47 runs in the final five overs, with Rinku Singh's 25 off 14 balls helping India move closer to the 200-run mark.

India finished on 192/5, a total that could prove competitive on a surface offering help to the bowlers.

title: 'Think about cricket, not social media': Ishan Kishan to Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
description: Ishan Kishan praised young Vaibhav Sooryavanshi after India's T20 win. He believes the 15-year-old possesses match-winning qualities for the national team. fullText:
Kishan'c comments came after India's 90-run win over Zimbabwe in the second T20I in Harare on Saturday. India were in early trouble after losing Abhishek Sharma (8) and Sooryavanshi (20) inside the first three overs, slipping to 29/2. Kishan then played a brilliant knock of 81 off 44 balls to guide India to 219/5. Zimbabwe were later bowled out for 129 as India sealed the three-match series 2-0 with one game to spare.

Kishan said the senior members of the squad are helping Sooryavanshi settle into international cricket and are encouraging him to ignore distractions away from the game.

"Vaibhav is actually very smart. He knows what he is doing," Kishan said after India's win.

"He knows how he has to bat and how he has to carry himself on and off the field."

The wicketkeeper-batter revealed that he, Abhishek Sharma, captain Axar Patel and other experienced players regularly speak to the youngster to ensure he remains focused.

"When you represent India, you have to know what to focus on," he said.

"Me, Abhishek, Axar bhai and many others keep telling him to think about cricket, not social media or outside noise."

Kishan said the team wants Sooryavanshi to learn from the experiences of the senior players and avoid getting distracted early in his career.

"When you have such a player and you know that he is very young, you will never want him to be distracted for the wrong reasons.

"So our job as a team, we are like brothers and he comes from my place, so we just have to be happy, focus on the important things. The mistakes we have made in our starting, he should not do that. He should enjoy his cricket, like he is doing now."

Kishan believes Sooryavanshi's attacking style can have a major impact on India's performances.

"If he stays on the pitch, the difference he can create for the team is huge. A player who can attack from the first ball can take you to 80-90 runs in the powerplay," he said.

title: How Abhijeet Dipke became the face of India's first Gen Z protest movement, and won
description: They were just six words posted on X in a moment of frustration:  "What if all cockroaches come together?"
fullText:
NEW DELHI, July 25 (Reuters) - They were just six words posted on X in a moment of frustration:

"What if all cockroaches come together?"

Now, its 30-year-old author, Abhijeet Dipke, is the face of what is arguably India's biggest street protest against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government ‌since he took office in 2014.

The political communications strategist's post, sent on May 16, was initially a witty response to comments by Supreme Court judge ‌Surya Kant, likening India's unemployed youth in a speech to "cockroaches".

Kant later said his comments were misconstrued.

A satirical platform called the "Cockroach Janta Party" (CJP) had sprung up, providing a rallying point ​for millions of young Indians frustrated over high unemployment and exam paper leaks and seeking greater government accountability.

Over the past week, tens of thousands gathered in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over leaks of the medical entrance test paper that affected some 2 million students in May and have been linked to several student suicides. Pradhan resigned on Saturday: a major victory for the young protesters and one of Modi's biggest defeats.

Protests were reported in other parts of the country too, including the financial ‌hub of Mumbai.

At the centre of it all is Dipke.

Based in the U.S. city of Boston until early June, he flew back to India to launch a protest near the Jantar Mantar observatory in the heart of Delhi.

Since then — and particularly after a police crackdown on demonstrators on Monday sparked public outrage — ⁠he has become a constant presence on a raised platform at the protest site.

Bearded and dressed in a T-shirt and jeans, Dipke addresses crowds of hundreds, urging them to remain peaceful while maintaining pressure on the government.

Even if the CJP has several organisers, Dipke has become its most recognisable face, drawing both admiration and criticism.

Dipke was born in Aurangabad in the western Indian ​state ​of Maharashtra into a Dalit family, one of India's most historically disadvantaged communities.

"My father comes from ​a very humble background. He grew up in extreme poverty. My ‌grandfather was just a farmer," Dipke told Reuters in May.

His Dalit identity has long shaped his politics.

When he arrived in Delhi on June 6, Dipke held aloft a copy of "My Autobiography" by B.R. Ambedkar, a champion of Dalit rights and key architect of India's democratic constitution, as supporters and security personnel swarmed around him.

In 2020, Dipke joined the social media team of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), where he said he developed a style of political messaging built around memes, humour and satire.

He is no longer associated with the party, though AAP and several other Indian opposition parties have backed the movement.

In 2023, Dipke moved to the United States to pursue a master's degree in ‌public relations in Boston, but continued to follow Indian politics closely.

FROM A SOCIAL MEDIA POST TO ​A MOVEMENT

Dipke says he is still trying to process his prominence.

One of the first people to amplify ​the movement was Delhi-based YouTuber Meghnad S. Soon after Dipke's post, he and ​a friend used AI tools to build a satirical website announcing the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party.

"I saw the page and ‌thought it was damn hilarious," Meghnad said.

The Instagram account amassed 22 ​million followers in a matter of days ​before swelling further to 25 million recently.

"That's how organic it was," Meghnad said.

But as the online movement grew, so did the stakes.

Speaking to Reuters from Boston in May, Dipke said:

"This is a movement to change the political discourse of India. The youth of India has largely vanished from the mainstream political discourse."

Despite threats ​to himself and his family, Dipke decided to return to ‌India. He has said he will stay at least until the students get justice.

Since June 6, Dipke has remained at the protest site as ​the demonstrations have swelled and can frequently be seen appealing to protesters to keep the movement peaceful, speaking to the media or grabbing brief ​naps.

title: Abhishek Sharma vs Blessing Muzarabani in T20Is: India batter's shockingly poor head-to-head record against Zimbabwe pacer

Abhishek Sharma vs Blessing Muzarabani in T20Is: India batter's shockingly poor head-to-head record against Zimbabwe pacer originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Abhishek Sharma has scored just 8 runs off Blessing Muzarabani across their T20I meetings.

The Zimbabwe pacer has dismissed the India opener three times in 21 balls.

Muzarabani's extra bounce has repeatedly troubled the left-hander at Harare.

Abhishek Sharma is one of the most destructive openers in world cricket, a batter whose fearless hitting has redefined how India start a T20 innings. Yet there is one bowler who has consistently found a way to shut him down.

That man is Blessing Muzarabani. The towering Zimbabwe seamer has turned his personal battle with Abhishek into one of the most lopsided head-to-head records in the format, and he added another chapter to it in the second T20I in Harare on Thursday.

The 6 ft 8 in (2.03 m) paceman removed Abhishek for the third time in T20Is, extracting the extra bounce that has repeatedly undone the left-hander at this venue and leaving his overall numbers against Muzarabani remarkably poor. In fact, in just this series, Muzarabani has dismissed Sharma in both the first and second T20Is.

MORE: India's 'Best Attitude Award' winners during Zimbabwe T20I series: Full list

Across their two years of meetings, Abhishek has managed just eight runs from 21 balls against Muzarabani while being dismissed three times, an average of 2.7 and a strike rate of 38.1.

The 2026 figures are especially stark. Abhishek has faced 14 balls from Muzarabani this year for just three runs, playing out 11 dots and failing to find the boundary even once against a bowler he would normally look to attack.

Thursday's dismissal followed the familiar script. Muzarabani conceded only three runs in his first two overs before Abhishek, struggling to hit through the line on a two-paced pitch, holed out to Brad Evans at third man.

MORE: 'Crush his confidence': Srikkanth slams Gambhir's treatment of Sooryavanshi

The mismatch is largely about height and bounce. Abhishek's game is built on hitting through the line and swinging across it, which works against bowlers who let the ball come onto the bat, but Muzarabani's steep bounce from a good length denies him exactly that. Harare accentuates the problem.

The surface offers early moisture and spongy bounce, and a bowler of Muzarabani's height extracts more from it than anyone, leaving Abhishek reaching for balls that climb higher than he anticipates. The contrast with his teammate is telling. Where Abhishek was tied down on Thursday, 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi took Muzarabani for a ride.

The youngster hit the seamer for two fours and a six in a single over, suggesting the answer lies in adjusting rather than in the bowler being unplayable.

That is the real intrigue heading into the second T20I. Abhishek remains far too good a player to stay quiet for long, but until he solves the bounce, this is a matchup Muzarabani will keep targeting every time the two meet.

title: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT
description:
Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
As a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers. Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say.
fullText:
As a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers. Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say. Your mum lives abroad. Avtar didn’t really pay any attention to it. “I thought, the neighbours are just making up stories.” But the stories were true: the woman raising Avtar was actually his grandmother. When he was too young to remember it, his father had emigrated to Canada to work as a teacher, leaving Avtar in the care of his paternal grandparents. His grandfather, a police officer, was a fearsome authoritarian, but his grandmother brought him up with tenderness, as if he were her own son. She called him by his nickname, Titu. He felt loved.

When Avtar was around eight years old, he was told about his family in Canada: his dad, his mum and a little brother were waiting for him there, and he would soon travel to join them. Just after his ninth birthday, Avtar found himself sitting on a plane, dressed in a three‑piece suit and tie. He was travelling alone. He had never flown before. He didn’t speak a word of English. He landed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Christmas Eve, 1968; his family met him at the airport and took him home. “I didn’t know what to think,” Avtar, now 66, tells me in a video call from his home in Abbotsford, British Columbia. “Before I knew it, it was the first week of January, and I was put in school.”

Unable to communicate with any of the other pupils, Avtar watched what they did and followed along, storing his snow boots in the cloakroom, standing up to sing the Canadian national anthem and God Save the Queen. But with his long hair tied in the topknot often worn by Sikh boys, he stood out. His parents offered to buy him a hockey stick and a pair of ice skates if he agreed to get his hair cut. He learned English. His nickname changed from Titu to the more Canadian “Tito”. He began to blend in.

But Avtar didn’t fit in at home. He was much paler than everyone else – “the white sheep of the family,” he jokes. And they treated him like an outsider, an afterthought. When he was 14, his family went on holiday without him, leaving Avtar home alone for two weeks. He got on well enough with his father, but didn’t gel at all with his mother. “She didn’t have any of the warmth that my grandma had. She absolutely hated me.” She seemed much more like a stepmother than a mother.

That feeling was confirmed when Avtar got married and his grandparents flew over to stay with him and his new wife, Rosie. His grandma “whispered into my wife’s ear” that Avtar was the product of his father’s first marriage. “She didn’t say what my mother’s name was. She just said, ‘Her family was from Africa, and she left the child with us and went back to Africa. She might have gone to live in the UK.’ That’s it.” It didn’t feel right to ask his grandparents 

When his son was set a school assignment to complete his family tree, Avtar felt emboldened to approach his father. “I said, ‘Dad, you’ve got to tell me at least what my mother’s name was.’” His dad eventually relented: her first name was Savinder. But he would not give Avtar any more information, no matter how many times he asked. “I was stonewalled.” Avtar had no idea why his parents had split up. “All I really understood was that my mother’s family encouraged her to give up custody of me so it would be easier for them to remarry her.”

He thought about his mother constantly. When Rosie was pregnant with their daughter, there were anomalies in some of the antenatal tests, and Rosie and Avtar were referred to a geneticist. Avtar was asked about his parents’ medical history. “I couldn’t tell them anything about my mother’s family history. It hit me right in the heart. That’s when I thought, I’ve got to do something.”

He Googled and Facebooked, but there was almost nothing to go on; Savinder is a fairly common Punjabi Sikh name. In 2009, Avtar flew to London to visit the National Archives at Kew with the hope of finding immigration or marriage records that might lead him to his mother. “I couldn’t find anything at all.” On a later visit to London, he emailed Sunrise Radio, a British Asian station, asking if they could put out an appeal to find his mother, but they told Avtar they don’t do that kind of thing, out of respect for people’s privacy. That gave Avtar pause. “I thought, maybe I should just cool off. If my mother has some other family, I don’t want to disrupt her life.” Still, it niggled. Three or four years ago, he asked a British south Asian work colleague for advice; she suggested contacting the ITV show Long Lost Family. He watched a few episodes and decided it wasn’t for him. But he longed to know his mother. “The thought of her did not leave my mind, ever.”

The one thing Avtar did not do was a DNA test. He is retired now, but he used to be a chartered accountant, and he knows enough about technology, data and privacy to be wary of giving up his genetic code to a corporation. “They can sell it. Not only that – if they see something in my DNA, that affects my kids. I don’t want that information up there.” He deactivated his Facebook account 12 years ago for similar reasons. “I don’t have faith that these companies have the proper safeguards.”

Then, on 8 May this year, Avtar and Rosie were on holiday in the south of France. Avtar had been battling cancer; their long-awaited trip to Europe came after he had finished his treatment. “It was early morning, and I had read all the news. I was bored. I had nothing else to do. I thought, I’ve tried Google and everything else, why don’t I give AI a shot?”

He typed a prompt into ChatGPT, based on the little he knew, and what else he could infer. He assumed that his mother would be around the same age as his father (who died 10 years ago); he knew that Sikh women of her generation were generally given the middle name Kaur.

Avtar Can you find any information about a Savinder Kaur?

Avtar She would be between 87 and 97 years old and would have lived in India and Africa and possibly in the UK

ChatGPT The strongest match, based upon your clues, is this …

ChatGPT Savinder Kaur Nagi, born in 1936 in Kisumu, Kenya, to Indian Sikh parents.

ChatGPT The article mentions family roots near Jammu and Kashmir in India and later migration connections to the UK.

“I know that AI can just make up shit. So I thought, OK, that’s nice says Avtar. “But it actually referenced an article. I thought, I’ll look at that, at least. Just to see.”

“I wrote it out of grief,” Nicci Dhamu tells me, in a cafe in west London. “Mummy never really had a voice, and that article was all about giving her one. I wanted to create a digital legacy for my mum.”

Nicci is the jewellery designer behind the brand Sohavi. “Sohavi means beautiful in Gurmukhī, the Sikh script. I learned about making things beautiful from Mum.” Her article, published on both the Sohavi blog and the South Asian Heritage Month website, was a celebration of her mother’s creativity. “She suffered loss, and decisions were made for her when she young and wasn’t able to assert her own voice, like many south Asian women of her generation. But she lives on through me and the profound influences she had on me throughout my life,” Nicci wrote.

Savinder Kaur Nagi died in her sleep in December 2024, aged 88. For the last five years of her life, she had dementia. Nicci, 58, had been her carer; they lived together and were very close. Nicci’s family moved to the UK from Kenya in 1973. She has an older sister and a younger brother, as well as three half-sisters from her dad’s first marriage; he was widowed before he met Savinder. “We grew up as one family. I didn’t know until I was about 10 or 11 years old that my sisters were my half‑sisters, and that was only because one of my sisters told me.” Theirs was a family that did not speak about the past.

“I remember once, Mum was in the kitchen making roti, and I asked her, ‘Mummy, you were, like, 25 years old when you got married to Dad. Wasn’t that a little old for somebody of your generation?’ I knew that something was different about our family, but I didn’t have the vocabulary to label it. My father never spoke to us about his wife who had died, and my mum never spoke about her life before him.”

When Nicci was in her 40s, an older cousin casually revealed that Savinder had been married to another man before she met Nicci’s dad. “She was married off, very young. And it probably wasn’t what she wanted,” Nicci tells me. “My grandfather took her and her sisters out of school in Kenya and took them back to Punjab to a place called Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar.” Later in life, her mother would openly lament leaving school – she could read and write English, and loved studying – but never explained why she had been forced to give up her education. She did not discuss her first marriage. She never told her children they had an older half-brother.

“My cousin told me in that conversation that she had a son.” Nicci’s eyes are bright at the memory. But she never felt able to ask her mother about him. “I couldn’t. There was intrinsic pain there.”

There were times, Nicci says, when her mother would sink into a depression. “She would sit quietly, or take to bed because she was upset.” Nicci would bring Savinder her dinner, and encourage her to sit up and eat. “Towards the end of Mum’s life, she used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘My child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for her.”

It was then – a couple of years before her mum’s death – that Nicci resolved to find the child her mother was crying for. But she did not know his name, and her mother was unwell so Nicci couldn’t ask her. Instead, she turned to her wider family.

She began with her mother’s young brother, who lives in Birmingham. “He knew my mum’s child as a two- or three-year-old,” Nicci says. She picked his brains, and also her cousins’. She learned that her mother’s first husband was called Mohan Singh, a very educated man who taught at the Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school in Amritsar. Mohan’s father had been a police officer, and “quite a difficult man”. Savinder had told her father that her husband wasn’t treating her well. “I think my grandad thought, this is not a good place for my daughter to be. He went around and took his daughter back to his home, and she must have picked up her little boy, too.”

Her mother raised the boy until he was three years old, Nicci was told. “As someone who is also divorced, I often reflect on the stigma my mother may have faced as a south Asian woman of her generation,” she tells me. “I think there was a lot of pressure from the family: let’s get her married. Somebody as young as her was going to have a very difficult life as a single mother. She was too young to be on her own. Her son’s family wanted him back. So they must have taken the child from her.”

Savinder returned to Kenya, alone. At first, she stayed with her eldest brother. Nicci’s cousins have vivid memories of her time in their home. “She would take his baby clothes out and cry. She never forgot him.” She was soon introduced to Nicci’s father, a man 16 years her senior. “I think she carried that trauma throughout her life, but did a very good job of holding her head up high, making her life work, raising three more children.” Family in Kenya heard “through the grapevine” that Savinder’s first husband had moved to Canada, but they couldn’t tell Nicci when. And no one knew the name of Savinder’s little boy. They only knew his nickname: Titu.

“No one’s going to call themselves Titu on LinkedIn, are they?” says Nicci with a deep laugh. That didn’t stop her trying to find him online, and his father and grandfather, too, Googling the names of teachers and police officers in Amritsar. “I didn’t capture anything. How do you find somebody without a name? It’s impossible.”

Three or four months before her mother died, she submitted Savinder’s DNA to Ancestry.com. “I set up a profile for her, saying, ‘Profile managed by daughter, looking for her son, name is Titu, possibly living in Canada.’” She got some interesting titbits back about her mother’s ancestral roots in Kashmir, Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, which would explain her light complexion, but no useful matches.

A month after her mother died, Nicci contacted friends who knew people who had worked for the magistrates court in Amritsar, in the hope of finding records of the divorce. “If there were divorce papers, there would be names – and maybe a child’s name.” But she was told that would be virtually impossible; a needle in a haystack.

In April 2025, Nicci’s family took Savinder’s ashes to India. During her stay in Amritsar, Nicci hired a driver to take her to Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school, where Titu’s father had been a teacher. She spoke to the teachers and the security guard, but it was long after Mohan Singh’s time there, so no one knew of him or his son. All she wanted was a name for her half-brother, but no one could tell her. It felt hopeless.

“I remember sitting there thinking, why doesn’t he just knock on the door? I knew that his father was an educated man – I was pretty sure that he must be educated, too. Why isn’t he looking for Mum?”

Avtar blinked at the article ChatGPT had presented to him. Rosie was just waking up. He made her a coffee and showed her what he’d found, but she wasn’t convinced. After all, the article didn’t mention Savinder’s first marriage, divorce or long-lost son. “Rosie didn’t want me to be disappointed – she knows how hard I had looked for my mother.”

Then he looked at the article again, and a picture stopped him in his tracks: not one of the many photos Nicci had posted of her mother – there was no flicker of instant recognition when he saw Savinder’s face – but an image of a certificate her mother had earned for dressmaking at a college in Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar, in 1962. (“She was so proud of it,” Nicci beams. “She would talk about it quite often: ‘I went to college, I earned a certificate.’ I think that was her quiet victory.”)

“This is two or three years after I was born, and it is in the exact city where I was born.” Avtar exhales deeply, as if he still can’t believe what he saw. He had to find out more. “This is the closest I’ve ever come. It would be a shame to just stop here.”

At 8.36am that morning, he sent Nicci an email, thanking her for writing the tribute to her mother.

Avtar What especially resonated with me was the part of her life connected to India. Reading about her journey raised many personal questions and reflections for me, and I found myself feeling there may be some distant family or community connections between us.

Avtar I want to assure you that I am not reaching out for any business, financial, or other formal reason, only in the spirit of a friendly conversation.

Nicci had spent the previous night praying at the gurdwara and watching Long Lost Family on TV. Avtar’s email had arrived on the morning of what would have been her mother’s 90th birthday. “It was wild!” Nicci exclaims. “I just had a real sense of knowing. I can’t explain it. This is my mum’s son. It’s got to be.”

She agonised over how to reply, eventually adopting a similarly friendly but respectful tone.

Nicci I am equally intrigued to know if there might be a family connection. I would be happy to have a conversation with you.

Her phone number was in her email signature. Avtar sent her a message on WhatsApp as soon as he saw it, asking when they could speak. Nicci scrutinised his WhatsApp profile picture. “He had a very distinctive nose. Everybody in my mother’s family has this prominent, distinguished nose.” She messaged back – she was free to talk there and then.

It was barely two hours since Avtar had typed his prompt into ChatGPT. He was driving with Rosie to get some croissants for breakfast. He parked up, clicked on Nicci’s number and called her. There wasn’t much of a preamble. Avtar was too eager to have his questions finally answered.

Avtar Good morning! This is Avtar Singh

Avtar When Is a good time to talk

Nicci I’m London based. As you probably know.

“Can you tell me a bit about your mother’s time in India?” he asked.

“Mummy was married and divorced in India,” Nicci replied.

“Yes,” Nicci said. “She had a son.”

Both Avtar and Rosie burst into tears.

“Titu, is that you?” asked Nicci. “Are you Titu, my mother’s son?”

“Yes,” Avtar replied. “That’s who I am. But I haven’t heard anyone pronounce my nickname that way since my grandma called me that, when I was a little boy.”

“At that moment, time just froze,” Avtar remembers. “But I quickly recovered. I said, ‘You’re my sister. Holy shit – are there more of you out there?’ It had never occurred to me that my mother would have a family, and that I could actually meet them. That family, they knew about me – everybody knew about me, they just wouldn’t talk about it – but I had no knowledge about them whatsoever.”

They spoke for two hours in that first phone call, until Avtar’s battery started to die. Nicci had assumed he must be in Canada; she couldn’t believe he was in France, so close by. “Why don’t you fly over?” she asked. Avtar’s head was spinning. They agreed to speak again later that evening, in a video call.

Avtar This was a dream of a lifetime!

Nicci then gave Avtar a tour of the family photos displayed in the living room she used to share with their mother. “I was just sharing everything I could with him. And sobbing. And remembering Mum. All that grief about her yearning to see him again, and not meeting him. It’s like the universe just flung something at me – although I’ve lost my mum, I’ve gained a brother.”

When Avtar told his son the news, he urged him to go to London and meet his newfound family. By the time he reached his daughter, she already knew: she had been using Avtar’s ChatGPT account and had seen his search history. “She said to me, ‘Dad, if you do not go see her now, you’re going to come back home and that’s all you’re going to think about. So go now.’”

Within days, Avtar and Rosie were in London. Nicci shows me a picture of the first time they met, at a hotel near Heathrow. Their faces are flushed with joy. “I could see the raw emotion in her – she had been looking for me for so long,” Avtar says. “When I met her and hugged her tight, I thought, yes, this is my sister.” They went out for dinner and compared stories and timelines, piecing together the fragments that their families had given them.

The following morning, Nicci took Avtar and Rosie to Birmingham, to meet their mother’s last-surviving sibling – their uncle – who had once shared a home with baby Titu. “He looked at me and said, ‘I remember you. I held you in my arms,’” Avtar tells me, his eyes awash with tears. “It was a great, great visit.”

The next day, Avtar was introduced to his half‑brother – Nicci’s youngest sibling. He had been shocked when Nicci first told him she had found Avtar. “He said, ‘But I’m Mummy’s son,’” Nicci tells me, laughing. “I said, ‘Of course you are. Nothing’s going to change our family.’ When they finally met, Nicci says her younger brother shook Avtar’s hand. “I just knew it was going to be all right. My brother said, ‘I’ve always wanted a big brother.’”

Avtar and Nicci both tell me they have no plans to confirm their relationship with a DNA test. There’s no need, they say.

“This world has a few billion people in it. And if somebody can randomly call me Titu … ” Avtar shakes his head. “I don’t think I need any more verification than that.”

The joy at finally finding Titu is bittersweet for Nicci, because it came too late for her mother. “My biggest regret is that I didn’t talk to her about her son and let her cry about him, let her have a release,” she tells me. “It wasn’t her fault. It wasn’t anything that she did wrong. It just was a marriage that broke down.”

“I grew up believing that she gave me up because it was the best thing to help her move on with her life. I was OK with that. I thought, I hope that she had a good life. I’m not the type of person to grieve or feel bad that I got abandoned or anything like that,” Avtar says. “Now I’ve heard from Nicci and other people in the family that my mum used to cry for me. That’s all I need to hear. It just feels so good to know that I was loved.”

Plus, Avtar adds, there is “the treasure my mother left behind for me – I have all this family to get to know”. Word about Avtar is slowly spreading across the globe. He’s in a WhatsApp group for his maternal family, including cousins based in Kenya; they have seen each other on FaceTime. There’s discussion of a trip to Kenya so Avtar can meet them in the flesh, and see where Savinder once lived.

“My cousins are so excited to meet him. He looks like them – same smiles, bald and bearded,” Nicci says with another throaty laugh. She whips out her phone to show me an AI-generated image Avtar has made of himself arm in arm with two cousins he’s yet to meet in person. Technology is bringing Savinder’s family together in ways she could never have envisaged, or even imagined.

“We had a video call last night,” Nicci says. “Every time I see him, I look at him and I just want to cry. That’s my brother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our lives.” She pauses. “Who would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.”

Her half-brother sees things differently. “Right now, AI is still a glorified search engine. It is a piece of software that recognises a pattern in a string of characters, and it can look at millions of responses that match that character set and give you the highest probability best answer. What did it do? It looked at a couple of character strings that I typed in and found the best match. There’s no intelligence there.”

Avtar remains as sceptical as ever about giving big tech his data, even though it was ChatGPT’s readiness to scrape blogs and give out personal information that led him to his maternal family. Had Avtar chosen to ask another AI, he might not have found Nicci at all. When he came back to Canada, he put the same prompt into Anthropic’s Claude, to see what it would say, just for fun. “It replied, ‘We don’t want to infringe on anybody’s privacy, so we don’t give out that information,” Avtar tells me. Then he shrugs. “I think that’s a good response.”

title: Australia open to playing Test against England in India
description: England and Australia should be open to the idea of playing a Test match in India to help generate interest in the format, says the chief executive of Cricket Australia.
fullText:
England and Australia should be open to the idea of playing a Test match in India to help generate interest in the format, says the chief executive of Cricket Australia.

The two sides traditionally only meet in Test cricket as part of an Ashes series, which is played on a home-and-away basis, with each country hosting it roughly every four years.

Australia and England are, though, poised to play a one-off Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in March 2027 to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the first meeting between the sides.

And Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg told BBC Sport the prospect of taking international cricket's most storied - and marketable - Test rivalry to India should be on the table.

Such a fixture would need buy-in from both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI).

"It's not something that we are planning, but it's open for consideration. We'd have to be open to considering all options," Greenberg said.

"Our relationship with the ECB and the BCCI is very strong and clearly there are opportunities in India to put more content in certain areas."

Cricket Australia is already looking to expand its footprint in India by taking the Big Bash League overseas for the first time, with Melbourne Renegades due to face Perth Scorchers in Chennai in December.

The governing body says the move is designed to grow the competition's global appeal by tapping into cricket's biggest market.

The popularity of Test matches in India have declined in the modern era amid a diet of T20 and the dominance of the Indian Premier League.

Greenberg said there was "no doubt" an England v Australia Test played on Indian soil would capture the imagination.

"I think Test cricket between us, India and England is very strong and probably bucking the trend in some other parts of the world. We want to make sure we grow and strengthen it," he said.

Greenberg defended the decision to stage the 150th anniversary Test against England under lights.

The centenary Test in 1977 was also played in Melbourne but this match will be the first men's Test at the venue to use a pink ball.

Some high-profile former Australia players are understood to have voiced their disapproval to Cricket Australia but Greenberg said it was not his job "to be popular".

"We wanted to get as many people for the game as possible. Playing that game in the day while people are at work and school would've made that difficult," he said.

"Clearly there's a commercial imperative with broadcast rights back in the UK and the time zone. Pink-ball Tests for us are hugely advantageous in terms of audience.

"It will anger some of the traditionalists but we're in the business of getting more eyeballs on our game."

Greenberg said Cricket Australia was trying to strike a balance between marking a significant milestone in the history of Test cricket and ensuring the longer format continued to move with the times.

He also indicated preparations for the match would produce a pitch offering a better spectacle than the one used in last year's Ashes Test at the MCG which England won inside two days.

"We're trying to balance celebrating 150 years of Test cricket between our two countries but also have an eye on the future and how we can evolve the sport," added Greenberg.

"We're trying to find that balance and hopefully the MCG pitch will be a little flatter than it was for the last Ashes.

"We certainly do have a good record in pink-ball Tests, but I think you'll find this one will be a bit flatter and have less grass on it, that's the intention."

India struggled against hard-length pace bowling during the T20I tours against Ireland and England, in which they failed to win a single game.

Zimbabwe's pace attack, led by Blessing Muzarabani and Richard Ngarava could exploit India in the same manner.

The Chevrons currently possess one of the most improved home seam attacks in world cricket.

Conditions in Harare could once again test India's batting against back-of-a-length bowling.

In a normal world, back-to-back T20 World Cup champions India would enter the three-match T20I series against Zimbabwe as clear favourites. However, after failing to win a single match across seven T20Is in Ireland and England, their aura has taken a significant hit.

New captain Shreyas Iyer is already under pressure to get India's white-ball rebuild back on track. While India will still start as favourites, Zimbabwe is no longer a side that the visitors can take lightly, especially if they replicate the blueprint that repeatedly exposed India's batters during the UK tour.

The Chevrons possess the weapon that could make life uncomfortable for the visitors.

Throughout the tours of Ireland and England, India's batters struggled against disciplined hard-length bowling. Pace bowlers who consistently hit the deck and extracted steep bounce found success, particularly on grounds with longer boundaries where mistimed pulls and cuts rarely carried to the fence.

Standing well over six feet tall with naturally high release points, both bowlers relentlessly attack the uncomfortable 8-10 metre hard-length area before mixing in steep bouncers that rush batters for time.

It is precisely the formula that troubled India throughout their recent white-ball tours.

Another seven dismissals came through short-pitched deliveries, which may have exposed India's inability to consistently dominate bowlers who refused to pitch the ball up.

Harare, though, is not the same as the UK stadiums but can offer a similar test. The venue has generally produced lower-scoring contests than the batting-friendly surfaces seen during IPL 2026, where 200-plus totals became a routine story.

That said, Zimbabwe's bowling threat isn't limited to pace alone. Veteran all-rounder Sikandar Raza remains the heartbeat of the side and could play a crucial role with his off-spin against India's left-handed-heavy top order.

title: 'Virat Kohli aur Rohit Sharma ko touch nahi kar payenge': Ashwin makes bold statement
description: Ravichandran Ashwin supports Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli's continued selection for India. He cited their extensive career achievements and significant fan support as key factors. Ashwin noted that bowlers do not receive the same level of public backing. Rohit Sharma recently silenced retirement speculation with a century against England. The captain stated that external criticism has always been part of his career.
fullText:
NEW DELHI: Former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin has thrown his support behind Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli, saying the two senior batters cannot simply be dropped if they still want to play for India. 

Ashwin's comments came after Rohit silenced retirement talk with a brilliant century in the third and final ODI against England at Lord's. Although India lost the match by 27 runs and the series 2-1, Rohit's 138 reminded everyone why he remains one of India's biggest match-winners.

Speaking on his YouTube channel Ash ki Baat, Ashwin said: "'Rohit Sharma aur Virat Kohli ko touch nahi kar payenge (They will not be able to touch Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma). They cannot touch Virat and Rohit if they want to play. It is because of their credentials. Rohit has scored almost 12,000 runs; they cannot touch him."

Ashwin said there was another major reason why the two stars are difficult to leave out.

"The other thing is, they cannot be touched because they are batters. They have an army, a battalion. People come to see them. If you drop them, it will just break the roof down."

Ashwin also pointed out that bowlers do not receive the same level of public backing as star batters.

"But if Shami, Siraj or Bhuvneshwar are not picked, 10 people will question. 100 people, 1000 people, maybe 10,000 people will question. But they won't make noise. If a day comes when people would make noise for bowlers, it would be difficult to drop them as well."

Rohit's place in the ODI side had come under intense scrutiny after reports claimed that the BCCI selection committee was not considering him for the 2027 ODI World Cup.

The India captain had scores of 11 and 26 in the first two ODIs against England before producing a stunning knock in the series decider.

Chasing 388 at Lord's, Rohit smashed 138 off just 110 balls, hitting 17 fours and five sixes. He kept India's chase alive almost until the end, even though the visitors eventually fell 27 runs short.

After the match, Rohit made it clear that speculation over his future has never affected him.

In an interview with BCCI.tv, he said external criticism has always been part of his career and that his only focus is performing for India.

"Look, my job is with the bat... Represent my country... That's what I'm gonna do. The noise... Since I made my debut, was there and till the time I'm gonna stay here, it's always gonna be there. So it doesn't really matter too much. What matters is what I do on the field," Rohit said.

title: India police use tear gas to stop march on Parliament by Cockroach movement supporters
description: Police used tear gas and batons to stop supporters of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement from marching to Parliament on Monday to demand the education minister’s resignation, while the government ap...
fullText:
NEW DELHI (AP) — Police used tear gas and batons to stop supporters of India's youth-led Cockroach movement from marching to Parliament on Monday to demand the education minister's resignation, while the government appeared to make its first outreach to the movement's leaders.

The police action came after thousands of demonstrators tried to breach security barricades surrounding the protest site in central New Delhi, marking one of the most serious confrontations in the movement's campaign against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government. Despite the crackdown, many protesters continued marching toward Parliament in small groups.

Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das accused authorities of "brutally cracking down" on "peaceful protesters." Delhi Police said the march had not been authorized and that restrictions were needed to maintain law and order around Parliament during the monsoon session, which began Monday.

The crowd at Jantar Mantar, a designated site for protests just a few kilometers (miles) from Parliament, included students, professionals and families with young children. As the day progressed, the gathering spilled beyond the protest site, with demonstrators filling surrounding streets and roads.

Many carried backpacks with water and food, expecting a long day. Others waved Indian flags as chants against the education minister and Modi rippled through the growing crowd.

The Cockroach Janta Party emerged in May, after the Supreme Court chief justice compared some unemployed young people to "cockroaches" during an unrelated hearing. Supporters embraced the remark, turning it into a satirical movement that has attracted millions of followers on social media.

The movement has gained momentum after repeated leaks of high-stakes entrance exams for medical colleges and government jobs sparked public anger. It drew wider attention after police forcibly moved hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to the hospital on Saturday.

Protesters calling themselves "cockroaches" have camped at Jantar Mantar for the past month, with members of several student groups joining Wangchuk's hunger strike. Thousands of supporters have also turned out at universities and rallies in other cities. They are demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, reforms to the examination system and compensation for the families of students who died by suicide following paper leaks.

Senior leaders in Modi's government have taken a hard line against the movement. Pradhan has accused the protesters of acting against the nation, while other ministers have acknowledged students' concerns but insisted there is no need for talks or negotiations with the movement.

Though that appeared to shift Monday, when representatives of the movement held talks with Health Minister J.P. Nadda. It was the first apparent sign of government outreach to protest leaders, who sought to bring their demands directly to lawmakers, prompting authorities to tighten security around the complex.

CJP spokesperson Das, who met Nadda, said he presented the protesters' demands, including the immediate resignation or removal of the education minister.

Separately, activist Wangchuk appealed for permission to temporarily leave the hospital and join the march.

In a handwritten note, he also said he would end his nearly three-week hunger strike only if the government took responsibility for failures in the education system and exam paper leaks, or if protesters were allowed to reach Parliament and lawmakers pledged to raise the issues in both Houses.

The protests have become a rare public challenge to Modi's Hindu nationalist government in its third term, drawing support from opposition parties, rights activists and some Bollywood celebrities. Protesters say space for dissent has shrunk under Modi, whose government has been criticized for suppressing public protests by jailing activists and, in some cases, using forceful police crackdowns.

Jyoti Rajput, a yoga teacher, said she joined the protests because "this rotten system refuses to take action."

"It cannot see the pain of students, and that's why so many people have joined this movement," she said.

For many others the campaign has expanded into a broader protest over government accountability. Some said they were driven by frustration with what they see as a lack of transparency and responsiveness from elected leaders.

Sneha Eppili, a 26-year-old protester, said she joined the demonstration because she believes the government has a responsibility to answer their questions.

"I voted for this government, so I think it's accountable to answer our questions. That's the basic human right that I deserve," she said.

title: What did England learn during ODI series win over India?
description: After beating India 2-1, BBC Sport asks if England are finally building momentum one year out from the World Cup.
fullText:
What a difference three weeks makes.

At the end of June, a dark cloud hung over the England camp, with Test captain Ben Stokes retiring after a 2-1 series defeat by New Zealand.

That campaign brought an end to coach Brendon McCullum's time in charge of the red-ball side, and plenty of questions remain about the future of the Test team, but the New Zealander has enjoyed an upturn in fortunes in July, with his limited-overs outfit beating India 4-0 in a T20 series and 2-1 in one-day internationals.

Defeating the world number one side in both formats, and overtaking them at the top of the rankings in the 20-over game, is no mean feat and England may feel they are now beginning to show the sort of momentum they last displayed in the build-up to their World Cup victory in 2019.

With the next edition of the tournament a little over a year away, BBC Sport takes a look at whether England's 50-over team is finally tracking in the right direction.

England's only significant change in the India series was a new opening combination of Ben Duckett and Jacob Bethell, and it bore fruit at Lord's.

The left-handed duo became England's sixth opening pair since the 2023 World Cup, with Phil Salt, Jamie Smith and Zak Crawley currently out of contention and Will Jacks and Rehan Ahmed considerations for the middle order after spells at the top.

They had a decent start in the first ODI at Edgbaston, putting on 63, but Duckett was dismissed first ball in the second fixture at Cardiff, with Bethell following shortly afterwards as England found themselves 8-2.

In London, however, the pair flogged a tired India attack, taking advantage of benign batting conditions to put on the highest ODI opening stand at Lord's, with Duckett pressing on for his fourth century in the format.

Bethell, who has not previously batted higher than four for England in white-ball cricket, started his ODI opening career with innings of 14 and four, but cut a composed figure at the Home of Cricket.

He played in a typically positive fashion, striking at 97.85 as he plundered 11 fours and two sixes before falling for 91, just short of a second ODI ton.

The 22-year-old's promotion up the order means England can carry an extra bowler, with the hosts fielding three seamers and spinner Adil Rashid alongside all-rounders Sam Curran and Will Jacks in the latter two matches of this series.

If England are to regain the World Cup, having surrendered it meekly in 2023, much of the responsibility will rest on Joe Root's shoulders.

The 35-year-old struggled by his standards in the one-day format for a number of years following the 2019 victory, averaging just 29 between 2020 and 2023, and his record saw him left out of the ODI set-up for the entirety of 2024.

However since his recall, Root has enjoyed a remarkable uptick in form, averaging 81.5 from 21 innings with four centuries.

He has now made six consecutive scores over 50, stretching back to the start of the series in Sri Lanka in January, becoming the first England batter to achieve that feat.

Root's unbeaten 76 at Edgbaston kept England in contention, with a 121-run partnership with Liam Dawson coming between collapses of 6-107 and 4-30, while an undefeated 99 in Cardiff anchored England's successful chase.

Coming in after the record-breaking opening stand on Sunday, Root enjoyed a rare opportunity to cut loose, with his strike-rate of 154.17 the highest of any ODI score over 50 in his ODI career.

If there is a question to be answered about England's side, it is who will fill the seamer slots in the XI.

With the World Cup to be played on the hard decks of South Africa and Zimbabwe, England will likely persist with three outright fast bowlers with the support of Curran.

Spearhead Jofra Archer is an automatic selection, assuming he remains fit, while Gus Atkinson did his cause no harm in his two outings against India, taking 3-50 in Cardiff and keeping to an economy rate of four at Lord's when no other bowler was under six.

The third slot remains up for grabs, with neither Josh Tongue nor Saqib Mahmood consolidating their place in the side.

Tongue took one wicket in two matches and was expensive at Lord's, conceding 43 runs from five overs, while Mahmood took 2-52 in Cardiff but was rotated out for Tongue for the series finale.

Brydon Carse returned to the squad for this series having recovered from wrist and elbow injuries that have kept him out of international cricket, while the selectors have also favoured the all-round skills of Jamie Overton and may return to him once he has recovered from the thigh injury he sustained in the Indian Premier League.

With a five-match Ashes series preceding the World Cup, England may expect at least one seamer to go down with injury, and will want a strong group of pacers ready to step up to the tournament squad.

There is also slight concern about spinner Adil Rashid, who has had a quiet 2026, taking eight wickets in ODIs and only one in this series.

The 38-year-old's economy rate for the year is consistent with recent efforts, remaining under six, while he can still claim to be England's biggest threat in overs 11-40 - taking 32 of their 72 wickets in that period since the start of last year.

England will return to the one-day format at the tail-end of the summer against Sri Lanka, with matches at Chester-le-Street, Headingley and The Oval between 22-27 September.

Their next taste of international cricket will be in the format as they play three matches in Australia in mid-November, before they sample World Cup conditions with three fixtures in South Africa in mid-January.

There is set to be an ODI series against Pakistan in the 2027 summer before the World Cup starts on 4 October.

title: England seal series with record Lord's ODI total
description: England hit the highest one-day international total at Lord's to beat India by 27 runs and seal a thrilling 2-1 series victory.
fullText:
Third one-day international, Lord's

England 387-3 (50 overs): Duckett 141 (135), Bethell 91 (93), Root 74* (48); Krishna 2-69

India 360-7 (50 overs): Rohit 138 (110), Shubman 77 (84), Kohli 74 (60); Curran 4-75

England won by 27 runs, won three-match series 2-1

England hit the highest one-day international total at Lord's to beat India by 27 runs and seal a thrilling 2-1 series victory.

Opener Ben Duckett made the biggest men's ODI individual score at the Home of Cricket in striking 141 off 135 balls as the hosts posted 383-7, surpassing the previous mark of 334-4 by England against the same opponents in 1975.

Duckett shared an opening stand of 192 with Jacob Bethell, who fell for 91, before finally chipping a return catch to Prince Yadav in the 44th over after smacking 18 fours and a six.

Joe Root helped drive England to their formidable total, hitting an unbeaten 74 from 48 balls for his sixth consecutive score of 50 or 

Asked to reach what would have been the second-highest winning target in the format's history, India remained in the hunt deep in the game thanks to Rohit Sharma's superb 138.

The 39-year-old, who is rumoured to be retiring at the end of the series, was in sparkling form, hitting 17 fours and five sixes in his 111-ball knock.

He put on his own stand of 147 with Shubman Gill, who struck 77 before he was trapped lbw by Adil Rashid.

Rohit's dismissal in the 38th over, bowled round his legs by Bethell, was the decisive moment in the match, leaving Virat Kohli to attempt to take India to victory as the required run-rate spiralled.

Kohli saw the remainder of the India middle-order dismissed cheaply, and he himself was then caught in the covers off the bowling of Sam Curran for 74, effectively ending the tourists' challenge.

India's tail continued to hit boundaries, but their target was too great and they finished on 360-7.
